### page_1
A palaeomagnetic study and age determinations of Tertiary rocks
in Nicaragua, Central America
S.-A. Elming,1 P. Layer2 and K. Ubieta 3
1 Department of Applied Geophysics, Lulea University of Technology, 97187 Lulea, Sweden. E-mail: sten-ake.elming@sb.luth.se
2 Geophysical Institute, University of Alaska, Fairbanks, Alaska, USA
3 Centro de Investigaciones Geoscientiﬁcas (CIGEO), the Autonomous University of Nicaragua (UNAN), Managua, Nicaragua
Accepted 2001 May 31. Received 2001 May 30; in original form 2000 February 4
SUMMARY
Palaeomagnetic, K–Ar and Ar 40 /Ar39 measurements have been made to elucidate
Nicaragua’s plate tectonic history. These show that the Nicaraguan Highland rotated
90u counterclockwise between 30 and 18 Myr ago, but the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain has not
rotated.
A lack of data has prevented a direct comparison with the tectonic history of adjacent
areas, in particular, the Chortis Block, which is the part of the Caribbean Plate that
is geologically most closely related to the Nicaraguan Highland. However, our data
suggest that the Caribbean Plate in this part of Central America was not consolidated
until c. 15 Ma.
Key words: Nicaragua, palaeomagnetism, radiometric ages, tectonic reconstructions,
Tertiary rocks.
INTRODUCTION
Nicaragua forms part of the Caribbean Plate (Fig. 1), which
is built up of a number of allochthonous terranes (Case et al.
1984) and has a complex geological history resulting from the
interaction between the North and South American, Farallon,
Cocos and Nazca plates. The present boundaries of the
Caribbean Plate are deﬁned by the distribution of seismic activity
(Molnar & Sykes 1969). Former plate boundaries evolved from
the relative positions of North and South America following the
Late Triassic–Jurassic break-up of Pangaea. In most Pangaea
reconstructions the area presently occupied by the Caribbean
Plate was overlapped by North and South America (Bullard
et al. 1965; Van der Voo et al. 1976; Pindell 1985), and the
Caribbean Plate is regarded as allochthonous to its neighbour-
ing plates. This means that North and South America are not
the rifted margins of the present-day Caribbean basin.
Duncan & Hargraves (1984) presented a model for the
evolution of the Caribbean in which the core of the plate was
formed from the lava that was poured out onto the Farallon
Plate when it moved eastwards over the Galapagos hotspot.
When the space between the Americas was big enough the
Caribbean entered the gap. Atc. 80 Ma the migration of South
America away from North America was more or less com-
pleted (Pindell 1985) and this may have been the time that the
Caribbean Plate entered.
Caribbean Plate boundaries have been predominantly either
strike-slip or convergent. Pindell & Dewey (1982) and Sykes
et al. (1982) suggest two distinct stages for the development of
the northern Caribbean Plate boundary. The ﬁrst is charac-
terized by a Late Cretaceous–Palaeocene northward conver-
gence, resulting in collision and suturing of the Antillean arc
with the Bahamas platform. This stage ended during the latest
Early Eocene–earliest Middle Eocene. The Caribbean Plate
then started to move eastwards relative to the North and South
American plates. The western part of this strike-slip boundary
evolved as a large pull-apart basin, the Cayman Trough. The
time of opening of the Cayman Trough has been estimated
at 45–50 Ma (Rosencrantz et al. 1988), and, from magnetic
anomalies produced by sea-ﬂoor spreading in the trough, the
rate of eastward movement has been estimated (Rosencrantz
et al . 1988). The trough opened at a rate of 20–30 mm yr
x1
from c. 50 to 30 Ma, when there was shift in the spreading ridges
and a slow-down of opening to less than 15 mm yr x1. This
probably reﬂects a reorganization of relative motion between
the North America and Caribbean plates.
As the Caribbean Plate is composed of various blocks and
microplates, a tectonic reconstruction of these is a basis for
the understanding of the formation of the Caribbean. Central
America can be divided into four major regions (Dengo 1969,
1985; Escalante 1990), the Maya, Chortis, Chorotega and Choco
Blocks (Fig. 1). The Chortis Block is deﬁned to encompass
southern Guatemala, Honduras, northern Nicaragua and
the western Nicaraguan Rise. This block has a pre-Mesozoic
continental-type crust, unlike the oceanic Chorotega Block in
the south. Central Nicaragua has been related to neither the
Chortis Block nor the Chorotega Block, while southwestern
Nicaragua may form part of the Chorotega Block (Di Marco
et al. 1995). The Chorotega Block constitutes most of the
southern Middle American landbridge and it has been suggested
that it formed the western edge of the Caribbean Plate during
the Late Cretaceous–Palaeocene (Di Marco et al. 1995). In an
Geophys. J. Int. (2001) 147, 294–309

attempt to understand Nicaragua’s plate tectonic context
(Elming 1983, 1985, 1992), our palaeomagnetic study was per-
formed together with K–Ar and 40Ar /39Ar age determinations
on predominantly Tertiary volcanic rocks from the central and
western parts of the country.
GEOLOGY OF NICARAGUA
Nicaragua can be divided into at least two different tectonic
regimes separated by the SE–NW-trending Nicaraguan
Depression (Fig. 2), which has been deﬁned as a half-graben
(McBirney & Williams 1965). The Cocos Plate subducts below
the Caribbean Plate with northeastward motion, and an
associated chain of volcanoes is located in the western edge of
the depression parallel to the trench.
East of the depression, Nicaragua is dominated by Tertiary
volcanic rocks of the Central American Highlands, which
extend SE–NW through the country. In northern Nicaragua
these volcanic rocks are superimposed on metamorphosed
Palaeozoic and Mesozoic rock formations. The volcanic rocks
can be divided into the Matagalpa and Coyol groups. The
Oligocene–Palaeocene Matagalpa Group volcanics are thought
to be deposited on an ignimbrite plateau (Ehrenborg 1996).
The Pliocene–Miocene Coyol Group, which consists mainly of
lavas, breccias, lahars and locally of pyroclastic rocks, has been
divided into upper and lower subgroups (Parsons Corporation
Report 1972), characterized by basaltic rocks overlain by inter-
mediate to acid volcanic rocks. Ehrenborg (1996) has explained
the repeated stratigraphic sequence using a facies model, relating
various volcanic centres to each other and superseding the
older subdivision of the Coyol Group.
To the west of the depression, in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain,
the rocks are predominantly of sedimentary origin and are
assumed to have been deposited on a Nicoya Complex type of
basement (Parsons Corporation Report 1972). The sediments,
tuffaceous shale, siltstone, greywacke, sandstone and lime-
stone, range in age from Cretaceous to Miocene (Rivas, Brito,
Masachapa and El Fraile formations) and are overlain by
sediments of similar composition to the El Salto Formation
and the pyroclastic deposits of the La Sierra Group (McBirney
& Williams 1965; Parsons Corporation Report 1972).
Seyfried et al. (1987) regard the Upper Cretaceous Rivas and
the Eocene Brito formations as parts of a continuous succession.
The Masachapa Formation is Oligocene in age (Auer 1942,
unpublished paper; Zoppis Bracci & Del Guidice 1958) and
the boundary between the Brito and Masachapa formations
has been interpreted as conformable (McBirney & Williams
1965). Also, the contact between the Masachapa Formation
and the overlying Miocene El Fraile Formation is regarded
as conformable (McBirney & Williams 1965; Kuang 1971) and
the El Fraile Formation interﬁngers with part of the volcanic
Tamarindo Formation.
The rocks of the Nicaraguan Highland are generally affected
by low-grade metamorphism of zeolite facies (Levi et al. 1987),

which means a temperature lower than 150 uC. Also in the
Paciﬁc Coastal Plain secondary zeolite and clay minerals are
found originating from alterations of volcaniclastics in the sedi-
mentary units (Levi et al. 1990). The secondary minerals show a
vertical zoning typical of burial diagenesis, which is a process
controlled by an increase in temperature with depth. A palaeo-
thermal gradient of about 15–20 uCk m
x1 is estimated for the
Cretaceous to Oligocene diagenetic episodes and the temper-
ature in the lower parts of the Rivas, Brito and Masachapa
formations is estimated at c. 120 uC. Mineralogical breaks
are observed between the Masachapa and Brito formations as
well as between the Brito and Rivas formations . These breaks
were suggested to reﬂect tectonic events of regional character
(Levi et al. 1990), possibly related to changes in the polarity of
subduction.
PALAEOMAGNETIC SAMPLING
Samples for the present study were collected from the
Nicaraguan Highland and from the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain.
The study includes some 245 samples from 30 sites (Fig. 3),
collected as block samples or with a portable drill, and oriented
with sun or magnetic compasses. Generally, each sampling site
represents a 10–20 m
2-scale outcrop. In the Highland, pre-
dominantly volcanic rocks from the Miocene Lower Coyol
Group and from assumed Oligocene–Palaeocene rocks of the
Matagalpa Group were sampled. As the tectonic control was
often poor, our ambition has been to collect samples of rocks of
similar age but geographically well-separated in order to detect
later local tectonic movements.
To the west of the Nicaraguan Depression we collected
sedimentary and intrusive rocks of the Rivas Formation, sedi-
mentary rocks of the Brito Formation and volcanic rocks of the
Tamarindo Formation. The ages of these formations are Upper
Cretaceous, Eocene and Miocene–Pliocene, respectively.
MINERALOGICAL STUDIES
Petrographic and X-ray diffraction studies (Nystro ¨m & Levi
1985; Elming 1985) have been carried out on specimens of
andesite, basalt and sedimentary rocks from a number of sites.
Most of the Tertiary rocks of this study are only incipiently
altered. As weathering is a particular problem in tropical
areas, martitization, the alteration of magnetite to haematite,
is a more or less common phenomenon. Martitization is here
developed preferentially on the grain surfaces and in the
crystals along lamella structures and in cracks. The degree of
martitization varies in the samples but is better developed in
rocks from some sites (e.g. sites 1, 3 and 6). Although the
remanent magnetization of haematite is usually more resistant
to demagnetization than magnetite, no signiﬁcant relation
between degree of martitization and directional variations of
the characteristic magnetizations was found. Magnetite is

however, magnetite of primary origin is the main carrier of the
remanent magnetization.
K–Ar AND 40 Ar / 39 Ar RADIOMETRIC AGE
DETERMINATIONS
In order to constrain the ages of magnetizations in this study,
we have dated samples from selected palaeomagnetic sites by
the K–Ar and
40Ar /39Ar methods. Previous Rb–Sr and K–Ar
dating of whole-rock and mineral phases (Zoppis Bracci 1961;
Barr & Escalante 1969; McBirney & Williams 1965) from both
the Highland and the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain were of poor
resolution and indicate that many of the units may have been
emplaced over a long duration. Dating the same samples and
ﬂows for which we have stable magnetic directions allows us to
avoid assigning ‘incorrect’ or estimated ages to the magnetization.
The K–Ar age determinations were made by R. M. Macintyre
at the Scottish Universities Research and Reactor Centre
(Table 1). One–four palaeomagnetic samples from each of the
11 sites 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16 and 17 were analysed,
including andesite and basalt from the Lower Coyol and
Matagalpa groups and a diabase dyke (Table 1). Basalts from
sites 12 and 14 and the basic dyke at site 10 are not identiﬁed
in the ﬁeld as being part of any speciﬁc group; however, based
on evidence presented here, we have assigned these sites to the
Matagalpa and Lower Coyol groups, respectively. From the
Paciﬁc Coastal Plain, ignimbrite and basalt were dated. One of
the dated basalts was associated with palaeomagnetic site 25.
X-ray diffraction analyses and observations from thin-
sections (Nystro¨m & Levi 1985) show that most of the samples
are relatively well preserved. However, these relatively unaltered
rocks do contain up to 10 per cent montmorillonite and zeolite,
minerals known to pose problems for K–Ar whole-rock dating.
This potential for disturbance can be seen in some of the age
scatter in sites where more than one age determination was
made. For example, samples from sites 9 and 10 (Table 1) show
signiﬁcantly different ages of samples from the same ﬂow.
Although K–Ar ages from the Lower Coyol Group tend to be
younger than those from the Matagalpa Group, the ages from
the two groups show large ranges and overlap. Thus it is
possible that either some ﬂows have been misassigned in the
ﬁeld or that the K–Ar dating systematics have been disturbed in
some samples due to alteration.
In order to assess the extent of alteration in the samples and
the reliability of the K–Ar ages better, selected whole-rock
samples were dated by the
40Ar /39Ar step-heating method. One
Figure 3. Location of palaeomagnetic sampling sites and sites sampled for Ar 40 /Ar39 and K–Ar age determinations.

sample was chosen from the Lower Coyol Group (site 10), two
were chosen from the La Batea Formation (sites 16 and 17)
and three were chosen from other localities of the Matagalpa
Group (sites 8, 12 and 14).
Samples were crushed and sieved and small chips from
the 100–250 mm fraction were chosen for dating. Samples of
Bern4B biotite with an assumed age of 17.25t 0.20 Myr were
used to monitor the neutron ﬂux. The samples were irradiated
for 2 MW h in position 5c of the uranium-enriched research
reactor of McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada.
The samples were step-heated from about 500 to 1600 uC.
The puriﬁed argon isotopes were then analysed in a Nuclide
6-60-SGA mass spectrometer at the Geophysical Institute,
University of Alaska, Fairbanks, USA. Argon puriﬁcation was
achieved using a liquid nitrogen cold trap SAES Zr–Al getter at
400 uC. The measured argon isotopes were corrected for system
blank and mass discrimination as well as calcium, potassium
and chlorine interference reactions following the procedures
outlined in McDougall & Harrison (1988). Plateau ages were
based on the criteria of three or more contiguous fractions
accounting for more than 50 per cent gas release having ages
within a 2s (95 per cent conﬁdence level) of the mean age.
For ﬁve samples (sites 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16), plateau ages
consisting of at least three steps totalling more than 60 per cent
gas release were calculated for each sample. Two samples
(sites 16 and 17) contained excess argon and an isochron was
ﬁtted to the data. For these samples an initial
40Ar /36Ar value
of c. 310 was found. A summary of all the 40Ar /39Ar results
is given in Fig. 4, with all ages quoted to the t1s level and
calculated using the standards of Steiger & Ja¨ger (1977). Detailed
geochronological data are available upon request from the
authors.

Paciﬁc Coastal Plain
One K–Ar age from a palaeomagnetic site of the Tamarindo
Group has an age of 12.3t 1.7 Myr for a basalt (site 25;
Table 1). Three additional samples from other locations of the
Tamarindo Group not associated with palaeomagnetic sites
have ages of 18.4t4.9 Myr (rhyolite ignimbrite), 15.4t0.5 Myr
(acid ignimbrite) and 13.7 t0.8 Myr (basalt) (Elming 1999).
The weighted average age for these samples is 14.8 t0.5 Myr.
Nicaraguan Highland
Eight of the 12 K–Ar age analyses of Lower Coyol rocks
are from basalt ﬂows and cluster about a single mode with a
weighted average age of 16.9t0.4 Myr. Of the remaining four
analyses, two (a 13 Myr age from site 11 and a 40 Myr age
from site 10) are not consistent with other more reliable samples
within the site and probably reﬂect argon loss or gain due to
alteration. Two samples from site 3 are from andesite rather
than basalt and they have an average age of 24.9 t0.8 Myr.
These ages are signiﬁcantly different from the average of the
basalt ages. It is not known if this difference reﬂects two stages
of volcanism in the Coyol Group or if the andesite samples have
incorporated excess argon and hence the ages are anomalous.
The spectrum of a single
40Ar /39Ar measurement from site
10 (Fig. 4) shows evidence of argon loss and the sample has an
integrated age of 17.5 t0.3 Myr. The integrated age of this
sample is similar to the average K–Ar age, which implies that
many of the Coyol samples may either have experienced some
argon loss or have been emplaced over a period of c. 2 Myr.
The plateau age of this sample is 18.5t 0.4 Myr and we
interpret this age to reﬂect more closely the true age of this
rock. In the absence of further geochronological information to
constrain the age of the Lower Coyol Group, we assign it an
age of c. 18 Myr.
The 13 K–Ar ages from the Matagalpa Group range from
about 18 to about 31 Myr (Table 1). 10 of the 13 ages form a
poorly constrained mode with an average age of 25.9t1.1 Myr.
It is probable that the samples of the Matagalpa Group reﬂect
multiple events (e.g. Ehrenborg 1996; Hodgson 1999) and an
average age of all sites is not geologically signiﬁcant.
Within the Matagalpa Group, the La Batea Formation
appears to be the youngest unit. Samples from sites 16 (basalt)
and 17 (andesite) of this formation have K–Ar ages of 25.8 and
17.8 Myr. Three samples were dated by the
40Ar /39Ar method.
Two of the samples show evidence of excess argon, probably
from a later alteration event. The average age for the basalt
unit (site 16) is about 23 Myr, while the age of the andesite
(site 17) is 19.6 Myr, signiﬁcantly younger.
Based on the palaeomagnetic evidence (presented below), the
remaining Matagalpa samples can be divided into two groups,
sites 8, 9 and 12, and sites 13 and 14. 11 K–Ar ages from the
ﬁrst group show a ‘bimodal’ distribution with two ages of
c. 18 Myr and nine ages scattering between 23 and 32 Myr,
with a mean K–Ar age of 26.5 t0.9 Myr. An
40Ar /39Ar age
of 23.80t 0.14 Mr is seen for a single sample from site 8,
consistent with the group of older ages. A sample from site 12
has an
40Ar /39Ar age of 17.61t 0.24 Myr, consistent with the
younger age group. These young ages are similar to ages seen
in ﬂows mapped as Lower Coyol, and it is possible that the
younger ages seen at these sites represent a second pulse of
magmatic activity.

### page_7
Samples from sites 13 and 14 form the second palaeomagnetic
group. The mean K–Ar age from site 13 (two samples) is
27 Myr, while an 40Ar /39Ar plateau age of 32.1 t0.2 Myr is
seen from site 14 (Fig. 4). Although it is impossible to assess the
amount of argon loss from samples of site 13, it is possible that
these samples are signiﬁcantly older than those from other
Matagalpa sites and have an age of c. 30 Myr.
Age summary
Based on our new geochronological evidence, most of the
samples dated by the
40Ar /39Ar method show either signiﬁcant
argon loss or signiﬁcant argon gain. If these signs of alteration
are prevalent throughout the sample suite, then interpretation
of the K–Ar ages is difﬁcult. Nevertheless, we can infer that the
age of the Tamarindo Group of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain is
c. 15 Myr, samples correlative with the Lower Coyol Group are
c. 18 Myr, the La Batea member of the Matagalpa Formation
is c. 20 Myr, Matagalpa sites 8, 9 and 12 are c. 24 Myr and
sites 13 and 14 are c. 30 Myr.
PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
The specimens were demagnetized by conventional alternating
ﬁeld (AF) and thermal demagnetization techniques and remanent
magnetizations measured with spinner and cryogenic magneto-
meters. The different components of remanence were deﬁned
by principal component analyses (Kirschvink 1980), and vectors
deﬁned with mean angular deviations larger than 7u have been
rejected. The site mean directions and formation means were
calculated using Fisher (1953) statistics.
It was possible to isolate well-deﬁned high-stability mag-
netizations in 26 of the 30 sites that were sampled. The results
from some sites were discarded due to very poor within-site
groupings of directions. Usually there were no more than two
components of remanent magnetization (Fig. 5), one of which
was of low coercivity with a direction similar to that of the
present Earth ﬁeld (PEF; D=0u, I=43u).
The Nicaraguan Highland
Rocks assumed to be of the Coyol Group or of similar age have
been sampled at seven sites (2, 3, 4, 7, 10, 11 and 18; Fig. 3).
The coercivity of the remanence varies but the soft portion is
generally erased at c. 20 mT (Figs 5a and b). Although the
number of samples in each site is often small, the directions
of the highest-stability component, referred to as the charac-
teristic magnetization (Butler 1992), usually form well-deﬁned
means (Table 2; Fig. 6a) and they are of predominantly
reversed polarity when compared to the PEF. It seems possible
to distinguish two groups of directions. One (sites 2, 3, 4 and 7)
is characterized by negative inclinations and the other (sites 10,
11 and 18) by shallow and positive inclinations. However,
the gradual change from positive to negative directions may
reﬂect a trend of changing magnetization ages, rather than two
distinctly different times of magnetization. Therefore, these sites
are treated together here (mean of sites: D=180.2u, I=x2.8u,
a
95=11.9u; Table 3), representing one magnetization age. On
the basis of the age data presented here, the age of magnetization
is estimated at c. 18 Myr.
The rest of the rocks sampled in the Nicaraguan Highland
are assumed to be of Matagalpa age, i.e. older than c. 20 Myr.
The characteristic magnetizations are of dual polarity; however,
reversed polarities dominate. The inclinations are generally
rather shallow, i.e. less than c.t30u, and on changing the mag-
netizations to reversed polarity the declinations vary from
c. 90u to 150uE.
The basalt and andesite of the La Batea Formation (sites 5,
15, 16 and 17) are all sampled from the central southern part
of the Highland. The characteristic magnetization is generally of
high coercivity and the blocking temperatures indicate the
carrier to be magnetite–titanomagnetite (Fig. 5d). At site 17 the
remanence is of lower coercivity, but the direction is still stable
up to 65 mT. Only at this site is the magnetization of normal
polarity. When changing the polarity of the site mean directions
to reversed, the declinations of the site means are quite similar,
while the inclinations are different. The fairly big differences
in inclinations may indicate local tectonic disturbances. As the
inclinations are shallow, declinations would be little affected
by tilting; however, we have no evidence of tilting from ﬁeld
observations. The site mean directions form a mean for the
La Batea Formation ( D=148.8u, I=5.9u, a
95=16.1u; Table 3)
signiﬁcantly different from that of the Coyol Group (Fig. 6c). The
whole-rock K–Ar and
40Ar /39Ar data suggest a magnetization
age for this formation of c. 20 Myr.
Matagalpa rocks were also sampled in the central parts of
the Highland (sites 8, 9, 12, 13 and 14; Fig. 3). These rocks yield
directions of magnetization (Fig. 6a) of reversed and dual
polarities, signiﬁcantly different from those of the La Batea
Formation. The declinations vary from c. 90u to 140uE and the
inclinations are predominantly negative and lower than c. 30u.
It is possible to distinguish two groups of directions with
signiﬁcantly different declinations of c. 130uE (sites 8, 9 and 12)
and 90uE (sites 13 and 14), respectively. The rocks of the two
groups are sampled from geographically well-separated areas
(Fig. 3).
The coercivity of remanence of the ﬁrst group varies but the
directions are fairly stable after being demagnetized in 10 mT
AF. The rock at site 8 carries characteristic magnetizations of
dual polarity, which may indicate that the rock at this site has
not been remagnetized. As for the La Batea Formation the
mean directions of the sites (Table 2) show that the inclinations
are different while the declinations are quite similar. The
direction of magnetization at one of the sites (site 12) of this
grand mean is also anomalous with respect to its
40Ar /39Ar age.
The mean direction for this group of sites is also very poorly
deﬁned ( a
95=40.2u; Table 3) and cannot be used to represent
any speciﬁc age of magnetization.
The coercivity of the characteristic magnetization of the
second group is usually high and in some samples the mag-
netization is of dual polarity (Fig. 5c), possibly indicating
a primary origin of magnetization. The two site means are
not signiﬁcantly different from each other and the directions
probably belong to a single population. The mean of the sites
(D=93.0u, I=x22.0u) is also very close to the mean of the
samples (D=92.9u, I=x17.9u, a
95=4.0u; Table 3). The age data
suggest magnetization ages for this second group of 30 Myr.
Basalt of only a few million years in age (site 6) has been
sampled off the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua (Fig. 3). This
rock carries a stable remanent magnetization with a direction
(D=346u, I=22u) similar to that of the theoretical dipole ﬁeld
(Fig. 6a; Table 2).

### page_8
The virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) positions (Fig. 7)
calculated from the site means and the grand means of the
Highland show the same trend of distribution as poles calculated
from Cretaceous rocks in Honduras (Gose 1985; Gose & Finch
1992). The centres of the polar arcs coincide with the sampling
region, which means that the distribution of poles may have
its origin in local structural rotations as well as plate tectonic
rotations (MacDonald 1978, 1990).
The Paciﬁc Coastal Plain
From the Paciﬁc Coastal Plains, basalt (site 25) and andesite
(site 26) of the Tamarindo Group have been sampled. The site
mean directions are of both reversed ( D=186u, I=x23u, site
25; Fig. 6b; Table 3) and normal ( D=356u, I=19u, site 26)
polarities and on inverting the polarity of one they are not
signiﬁcantly different. After removing a soft component of
remanence with a direction similar to that of the PEF, the
magnetization of the basalt is of high coercivity and the
directions are stable up to 100 mT AF (Fig. 5e). The portion of
soft remanence is much smaller in the andesite and a stable
magnetization is isolated after treatment in c. 25 mT AF. The
mean direction of the two sites ( D=0.9u, I=21.1u) is not
signiﬁcantly different from the mean of the samples ( D=2.0u,
I=21.6u, a
95=3.2u; Table 3). The Tamarindo Group is regarded
as equivalent to the Coyol Group of the Highland and an age of
c. 15 Myr is estimated for the magnetization on the basis of the
age data presented here.
Sedimentary rocks of the Brito Formation have been
collected at ﬁve sites and at four of them (21, 22, 23 and 24;
Fig. 3) a characteristic magnetization could be deﬁned. Bedding
correction has been performed and the mean directions pre-
sented here all refer to directions after structural correction. At
sites 23 and 24, samples were taken from stratigraphic intervals
of 7 and 5.5 m, respectively. The sandstone and shale at site 23
often carry a large portion of low-blocking-temperature ( T
b)
components erased at temperatures below 200uC and a charac-

and 450 uC. This magnetization, which is of reversed polarity,
was deﬁned during thermal demagnetization in 10 of the 24
samples collected at this site. No stable magnetization was
isolated during AF demagnetization. The bedding dipsc. 13uSW
and the corrected mean direction (D=176u, I=6u; Table 2) has

At site 24 two or three different components of magnetization
can be identiﬁed during AF demagnetization. The coercivity
of remanence varies in the sandstone samples and is lower
in the intermediate part of the stratigraphic sequence. In the
lower parts, the coercivity spectrum, expressed by the medium
destructive ﬁeld (MDF) (Dunlop & O ¨zdemir 1997), varies
between 10 and 23 mT and three components have been isolated
(Fig. 5f). A soft magnetization with a direction not far from the
theoretical dipole direction is erased in 15 mT AF. A second
component is isolated in 20–50 mT AF and 350–450uCt h e r m a l
treatment; however, the mean direction of this magnetization
(site 24a, D=10u, I=28u; Table 2) is not signiﬁcantly different
from the mean direction of the soft component. A third
direction is isolated after demagnetization in 40–100 mT AF.
The direction of this magnetization ( D=9u, I=4u; Table 2) is
signiﬁcantly different from those of lower coercivities. For some
samples the trajectories in the vector diagrams do not pass
through the origin (Fig. 5f), which indicates the existence of an
undeﬁned magnetization. At increasing AF demagnetization
levels the directions in these samples change along great-circle
paths. The remagnetization circles were analysed using the
method of Halls (1976) and the great circles intersect at a
declination and inclination of D=191.1u, I=x12.5u, which
suggests the existence of a reversed-polarity high-coercivity
magnetization.
The characteristic magnetization carried by the sandstone
at site 21 ( D=192u, I=x17u; Table 2) is isolated during
thermal demagnetization at temperatures above 500uC. A low-
temperature component with a direction similar to that of the
PEF was erased at temperatures below 400 uC.
The site mean direction for site 22 is poorly deﬁned (D=15u,
I=7u, a
95=24.4u; Table 2). The characteristic magnetization is
isolated at temperatures of 450 uC and higher. The directions
are of mixed polarity and imperfect cleaning and isolation of
the different components may be the reason for the poorly
deﬁned mean direction.

and the high-coercivity component at site 24 were used to

for the mean, the precision parameter is lower ( k=23.9).
This probably indicates that the high-coercivity component is
primary and that the intermediate-coercivity component is of
secondary origin. Gose (1983) reported palaeomagnetic results

Two basic rocks (sites 19 and 20) intruding the Rivas
Formation were sampled. At site 19 the basic dyke carries a
remanence of rather low coercivity (MDF=8 mT); however, a
characteristic magnetization can be deﬁned after AF cleaning
in ﬁelds higher that 15 mT. The mean direction ( D=356u,
I=34u; Fig. 6b; Table 2) is of normal polarity and not far from
that of the PEF. In one sample a high-coercivity component of
reversed polarity is isolated.
The coercivity of the characteristic magnetization in the
basic sill at site 20 is high (MDF =35 mT) and the direction
is stable after erasing a soft component with a direction close
to that of the PEF. The direction of the characteristic mag-
netization is of reversed polarity (D=184u, I=x23u; Table 2).
The fact that there are mixed but predominantly normal
polarities at site 19 and reversed polarities at site 20 suggests
that the magnetizations are not a result of remagnetization. The
mean of the sites (D=0.2u, I=28.6u; Table 3) is not signiﬁcantly
different from the mean of the samples (D=0.9u, I=27.7u). The
basic sill has been radiometrically dated at 50 Myr (K–Ar; Barr
& Escalante 1969). Gose (1983) collected sandstone samples at
two sites from the Rivas Formation. After structural correction
the site mean directions (G1: D=353u, I=32u;G 2 :D =2u,
I=22u; Table 2) are very close to the site means of this study.
The K–Ar age of the basic sill is signiﬁcantly younger than the
assigned Upper Cretaceous age of the Rivas Formation. This

The palaeomagnetic poles calculated from the grand mean
poles of the Tamarindo, Brito and Rivas formations all cluster
around the geographical pole.
ORIGIN OF MAGNETIZATION
The pole positions calculated from the characteristic mag-
netizations of the rocks in the Highland and the Paciﬁc Coastal
Plain sometimes fall close to the geographical pole, which may
imply that the rocks have been remagnetized.
Mineralogical studies of rocks from the Highland indicate
only low-temperature ( j120 uC) burial metamorphism and
predominantly unaltered magnetite as the magnetic mineral.
Also, the palaeomagnetic study shows that magnetite is the
dominant carrier of remanence. Usually there are only two
components of magnetization even though the coercivity and
blocking-temperature spectra are often rather wide (e.g. Fig. 5d).
The soft components often have directions similar to that of the
PEF, indicating this magnetization to be a viscous remanence.
In the Highland there are remanent magnetizations of both
polarities and at some sites there are magnetizations of mixed
polarity. Although reversals are no guarantee of a primary mag-
netization, they support an interpretation of a primary origin
of the characteristic magnetizations (Van der Voo 1990). The
burial metamorphism seems not to have affected the primary,
high-blocking-temperature magnetization of the rocks, although
it is probably the reason for the disturbed K–Ar system
resulting in the wide scatter of the measured K–Ar ages.
Also in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain, the rocks have been
affected by burial metamorphism, but the temperatures did
not exceed c. 120 uC. Due to probably slow erosion and uplift
this relatively low temperature may have affected grains with
laboratory unblocking temperatures of some 250 uC (Pullaiah
et al. 1975). Both Rivas and Brito sediments are volcanogenic,
which means that magnetite may be expected as a carrier of a
detrital remanence. This is also supported by the unblocking
temperatures of the Brito sandstone and shale. A large portion
of the remanence is erased at temperatures below 250 uC
and the characteristic magnetization is deﬁned in the temper-
ature range 300–580 uC. This means that the characteristic
magnetization is probably a detrital magnetization not affected
by burial metamorphism. The Brito sedimentary rocks carry
magnetizations of dual polarity and Gose (1983) reported a
magnetostratigraphic zonation of normal and reversed polarities
in the Brito Formation, which most probably rules out the
possibility of remagnetization. When structural correction is
performed the precision of the mean direction for the Brito
Formation increases, as indicated by the ratio of the precision
parameters after ( k
2) and before ( k1) correction ( k2 /k1=
1.83–2.49). Even if this increase is not sufﬁcient to show that
Figure 7. Palaeomagnetic pole positions of Tertiary rocks from the Nicaraguan Highland (this study) (marked by triangles) and Cretaceous rocks
from Honduras (Gose 1985; Gose & Finch 1992) (marked by crosses). Open symbols denote poles of reversed polarity and the ﬁlled symbols A and B
denote the 30 and 60 Myr reference poles for North America. Grand mean poles are marked by dots and shown with their circles of conﬁdence (A95).

### page_13
the magnetization pre-dates folding at the 95 per cent con-
ﬁdence level, it adds credibility to the data. Gose (1983) argues
for a primary origin of the detrital magnetization in the Rivas
sandstone, on the basis of palaeomagnetic data, and a volcano-
genic origin for the carrier of remanence. Also, the basic rocks
intruding the Rivas Formation carry magnetizations of dual
polarity, which supports the interpretation of a primary origin
of the magnetization.
For the magnetization of the volcanic rocks, secular
variations of the magnetic ﬁeld must be considered. These
variations are probably averaged out when the grand means are
calculated from four site means or more. Three of the grand
means are based on only two site means. In the Paciﬁc Coastal
Plain the two basic rocks (sites 19 and 20) intruding the Rivas
Formation and the andesite and the basalt from the Tamarindo
Formation (sites 25 and 26) have magnetizations of dual polarity.
These magnetizations are very close to being antipolar, which
suggests only minor deviations from a dipole ﬁeld. The third
grand mean calculated from only two site means is for the
c. 30 Myr old rocks from the Nicaraguan Highland. At one of
these sites (site 14) the rock carries a magnetization of mixed
polarity, suggesting that it was not extruded at the same time as
the rock at the other site. Nonetheless, the directions are not
signiﬁcantly different, which possibly indicates secular variations
only within the error bars of mean direction.
INTERPRETATION AND DISCUSSION
The interpretation of the palaeomagnetic data of this study is
based on the premise that the magnetizations are primary.
As the tectonic control of the rocks in the Highland is poor,
the directions referred to here are in situ directions. This may
also be the reason for the sometimes quite large differences
between inclinations of the site means, which then form
poorly deﬁned grand mean poles. The 24 Myr grand mean pole
(Table 3) is discarded due to the very poor precision in the
mean direction. The tectonic reconstructions should therefore
here be regarded as tentative.
In the Nicaraguan Highland, data from volcanic rocks older
than c. 18 Myr are sparse and together with the lack in
structural control, this implies that local block rotations cannot
be excluded as a source of the rotation indicated by the
palaeomagnetic data. A large block delineated by well-deﬁned
fracture zones has been deﬁned in the northeastern part
of Nicaragua (Leyton 1994), but no signs of rotation were
observed. Normal and to some extent strike-slip faulting
has been reported from geological mapping of the Highland
(Ehrenborg 1996), but no evidence of structural rotations.
Rocks of similar ages and directions of magnetization have
been sampled at geographically well-separated sites (e.g. the
La Batea Formation). This means that the rotations, indicated
by the gradual change in declinations and pole positions
(Figs 6 and 7) with increasing age of the rocks, should not
originate from local blocks. We therefore suggest that the
rotation indicated from the data in the Nicaraguan Highland is
a plate tectonic rotation. From the comparison of VGPs with
those of North America (Fig. 7) it is evident that this rotation,
which took place between c. 30 and 18 Ma, is counterclockwise
and c. 90u (Fig. 8). The rate of rotation, 7.5uMyr
x1, is high and
may be an artefact due to the problem of determining the exact
magnetization ages.
Gravity data (Ubieta 1995; Elming & Rasmussen 1997)
indicate that the Mesozoic–Palaeozoic crust of the Chortis
Block continues southwards beneath the Tertiary cover of
volcanic rocks to the central parts of the Highland and westwards
to the Nicaraguan Depression. Pb isotope data (Sundbladet al.
Figure 8. (a) Tentative tectonic reconstructions of the Nicaraguan Highland (NH) and the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain (PCP) during the Tertiary and
(b) palaeopositions of the Maya (MB) and Chortis (CB) blocks during the Late Cretaceous modiﬁed from Gose (1985). The areas related to the
Chortis Block, the Nicaraguan Highland and the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain are deﬁned by vertical, horizontal and inclined lines, respectively, in (c).
306 S.-A. Elming, P. Layer and K. Ubieta
# 2001 RAS, GJI 147, 294–309
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/gji/article/147/2/294/717705 by Curtin University Library user on 29 April 2026

### page_14
1991) suggest a Mesozoic–Palaeozoic crust in the Nicaraguan
Highland. Unfortunately there are very few Tertiary palaeo-
magnetic data from the Chortis Block and a direct comparison
with the data from the Nicaraguan Highland is therefore not
possible.
A large counterclockwise rotation of the Chortis Block
during the late Cretaceous was demonstrated by Gose (1985)
and at c. 60 Ma the orientation of the Chortis Block was c. 30u
different from the present orientation with respect to North
America (Fig. 8)
From the development of the northern Caribbean Plate
boundary, a change from northwards convergence to east-
wards movement of the Caribbean Plate relative to North
America in the Middle Eocene was suggested (Pindell & Dewey
1982; Sykes et al . 1982). This coincided with the opening of
the Cayman Trough some 45–50 Myr ago (Rosencrantz et al.
1988). At c. 30 Ma there was a shift in the spreading ridge and
a slow-down of the opening, which may reﬂect a change of the
relative motion between the Caribbean and North American
plates.
Our data indicate a counterclockwise rotation of the
Nicaraguan Highland from c. 30 Ma to the present. This may
be explained by left-lateral shear in the northern plate boundary
related to continuing eastward motion of the Caribbean Plate
and related blocks. On the basis of palaeomagnetic data from
the Caribbean, most of the rotations along the plate boundaries
took place in the Tertiary, commonly in post-Eocene time
(Gose 1985). If the Nicaraguan Highland was part of the
Chortis Block, this means that between c. 60 and 30 Ma this
block must have rotated 60 u clockwise to ﬁt the tectonic
reconstruction of the Highland. This is not supported by the
trend of counterclockwise rotation for the Chortis Block
during the Middle Cretaceous to Early Tertiary as suggested by
Gose (1985) and may indicate that the Nicaraguan Highland
acted as an independent block, separated from the Chortis
Block by a prominent fault zone, for example, the Guayape
Fault in southern Honduras. If this is correct the southwestern
boundary of this block may coincide with the Nicaraguan
Depression and the southern boundary would be located south
of 12u latitude, possibly coinciding with the Hess Escarpment.
A counterclockwise rotation of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain
since the Miocene was suggested from a palaeomagnetic study
of a basaltic dyke (Sick 1989). However, palaeomagnetic poles
of the present study calculated from Upper Cretaceous and
Tertiary rocks of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain do not reveal
any signiﬁcant indication of rotation. The poles of the Rivas,
Brito and Tamarindo formations cluster around the geo-
graphical pole. Palaeomagnetic studies in Costa Rica (Di Marco
et al . 1995) of rocks similar to those of the Paciﬁc Coastal
Plain showed that no rotations of the Chorotega Block took
place during Cretaceous–Tertiary time. From the similarity in
neotectonic evolution, Weinberg (1992) suggested that northern
Costa Rica and western Nicaragua were part of the same
tectonic block at least since the Miocene and no major breaks
separated the two areas. Di Marco et al. (1995) also suggested
that southwestern Nicaragua forms part of the Chorotega
Block.
The counterclockwise rotation of the Nicaraguan Highland
ceased at c. 18 Ma, as indicated by the pole calculated for the
Coyol Group (Table 3; Figs 7 and 8). This coincides with the
time of the ﬁrst deformation of the sediments of the Paciﬁc
Coastal Plain (Cruden 1989; Weinberg 1992) and the change in
volcanism from the volcaniclastic Matagalpa Group to the
andesitic Coyol Group. The Tamarindo Formation (c. 15 Myr)
in the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain is equivalent to the Coyol Group
(Weyl 1980) and the calculated poles are similar but of opposite
polarity (Table 3). This, in conjunction with uplift and defor-
mation of the fore-arc sedimentary basin, may indicate accretion
of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain and the Chorotega Block to the
Nicaraguan Highland 15–18 Myr ago.
The palaeolatitudes, as calculated from the inclinations of
the formation mean directions, vary. These variations may
partly be due to the poor tectonic control in the Nicaraguan
Highland, reﬂected by the sometimes large conﬁdence cones
of the mean directions, and the interpretation is therefore
tentative. The calculated positions of the Highland and the
Paciﬁc Coastal Plain are in most cases around the equator or at
low northern latitudes (3 uS–11uN).
CONCLUSIONS
The palaeomagnetic data of this study indicate a tectonic
history of the Nicaraguan Highland completely different from
that of the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain. This means that Nicaragua
cannot be regarded as having been a coherent tectonic unit.
From the similarity in palaeomagnetic directions it is
suggested that the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain and the Chorotega
Block were joined during the Tertiary. The change in crustal
composition from continental to oceanic when moving from
the Highland to the Nicaraguan Depression may support a
different tectonic origin of the Highland and the Paciﬁc Coastal
Plain.
The lack of palaeomagnetic data from Tertiary rocks
from Honduras or other parts of the Chortis Block prevents
a direct comparison with the tectonic history of the Nicaraguan
Highland. Even if the Mesozoic–Palaeozoic crust of the Chortis
Block seems to continue southwards into the Nicaraguan
Highland, it is still not clear if the Highland was part of the
Chortis Block in the Tertiary.
Our palaeomagnetic data suggest that the Caribbean Plate
in this part of Central America was not consolidated into its
present shape until c. 15 Ma. The rotation of the Nicaraguan
Highland then ceased and the Paciﬁc Coastal Plain and the
Nicaraguan Highland amalgamated.
ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
We wishes to thank G. Hodgson at the former Nicaraguan
Ministry of Mines (INMINE) for geological advice and help
with ﬁeldwork. Thanks are also due to M. McWilliams for
letting us use the palaeomagnetic laboratory at Stanford. This
project was supported ﬁnancially by the Swedish Agency for
Research Cooperation with Developing Countries (SAREC).
